note: Fixed offered rates, identical for every target in every language, published as real times rather than as a ratio to anything. docs/measurement-v2.html is the design, and ladder-v2 is its ladder of two rates. ladder-v2's rates are chosen from the traffic a reader might want to serve, not from where the targets break: set from the population they would move every time a language is added, and moving them breaks the time series. Its 1000 and 5000 are provisional until the dedicated machine has run. The nightly runs this ladder on a GitHub-hosted runner. It differs from ladder-v2 in three ways. Its durations are shorter, so the container job fits inside measure.yml's timeout-minutes: ladder-v2 warms for 90s (jit) and 30s (steady) and runs each rung for 240s. Its first two rates are half of ladder-v2's, because 26 of the 33 targets did not complete 5000 on that runner (#95). It adds a third rate at 5000, so the frameworks that hold 5000 still show it.

warmup.note: serial_requests is the serial suite's equivalent of seconds. A rate ladder warms for a duration; a host that runs one invocation at a time warms for a count, and a JVM needs thousands of invocations to reach C2 rather than the few hundred a steady runtime needs.
warmup.ramp_note: The warmup is recorded and published as a ramp: the first request on its own, then the whole latency distribution for each slice of the schedule, one second wide until fine_until_s and ten seconds wide after it. That makes rps, seconds, slices and first protocol rather than tuning. Changing one breaks the ramp series the way moving a rung rate breaks the rung series, so it takes a new ladder version rather than an edit. json.small goes first because the readiness probe has already taken the plaintext path.

rungs.name: regular
rungs.purpose: traffic every target is expected to serve; this is where latency is compared

rungs.name: raised
rungs.purpose: traffic that separates the frameworks with headroom from the ones without

rungs.name: peak
rungs.purpose: traffic that only the frameworks with the most headroom hold

abort.note: Watched during the settle window, which is unrecorded anyway. A target dropping this much fifteen seconds in drops it a minute in, so the remaining sample is spent to learn nothing. The settle doubles as the probe, so a target that passes pays nothing for the check.

publish.note: A blend is published only where the target completed the rate. gen/blend.mjs drops by never sending, so a dropped request never enters a histogram and the percentiles are computed over survivors: the requests excluded are the ones that would have been slowest, and a framework that collapses reports a better p99 than one that degrades gracefully. Where this is exceeded the row carries achieved rps and the drop count instead of a latency.

min_requests_note: What the ladder actually delivers, rather than a floor it has never met. Rung 1 is 500 rps for 60s, so 30,000 requests across 50 endpoints is 600 each, with room for about ten more endpoints before it binds. At this length a per-endpoint p99 rests on about six observations. ladder-v2's 240s rung delivers 4,800 each and sets this to 4,000.
